cards.front: Message rate for 100M users sending 50 messages a day
cards.back: 5B a day, about 58,000 a second on average and about 170,000 at the evening peak.

cards.front: How many gateways for 25M open connections?
cards.back: At about 200k idle sockets per tuned server, 125 gateways, about 170 with headroom for a zone failure. Memory, not CPU, is the limit.
One long-lived connection lets the server push the moment a message arrives. Polling wastes battery and adds latency.
Only open connections and which user each belongs to. It is the only stateful tier, so it is kept dumb and easy to replace.
The server assigns each message the next integer sequence number for its conversation. Phone timestamps drift and tie, so they can't order messages.

cards.front: How a retried send avoids duplicates
cards.back: The client sends a random client_msg_id; the chat service checks a short-lived dedupe set and replies 'sent' again for a repeat.

cards.front: When does the sender see one tick?
cards.back: Only after the chat service assigns the sequence and writes the message durably.

cards.front: Sync by position, not by push
cards.back: On every connect a device asks for messages after seq N in each conversation and fills gaps from the store. A missed push delays a message but never loses it.
Mobile networks and NAT gateways silently drop idle connections. Pings keep the path open and let the registry entry expire when they stop.
Partition by (conv_id, bucket), cluster by seq, so 'messages after 4100 in this chat' is one contiguous range read.
Heartbeats refresh a Redis key with a 60 s TTL; clients subscribe to presence only for chats on screen, and changes are debounced.
A mailbox, not an archive: a message is stored only until every recipient device acknowledges it, then deleted. History lives on the phones.

quiz.q: A gateway holding 200k connections crashes, and the remaining gateways and the registry overload one after another. What should have prevented it?
choices: Clients reconnecting with exponential backoff and random jitter
quiz.why: Jitter spreads the reconnect herd over tens of seconds so the overload doesn't spread.

quiz.q: Two group members see messages in a different order. The client sorts by the sender's phone timestamp. What is the fix?
choices: Sort by server receive time on the gateway
A per-conversation sequence number assigned by the server
quiz.why: Clocks drift and tie; a server-assigned integer per conversation gives one order everyone shares.

quiz.q: A push frame to a recipient is lost because their gateway restarted. What guarantees they still get the message?
choices: On reconnect the device syncs everything after its last seq from the store
The chat service retries the push forever
Kafka replays all messages to every device
quiz.why: Correctness rests on sync by position, not on the push.

quiz.q: During a network split, each region keeps numbering a conversation independently. What goes wrong?
choices: Two different messages both get seq 4183 and devices disagree for good
quiz.why: Each conversation needs one home region owning its counter; queue on the client instead of inventing numbers.

quiz.q: Presence traffic outnumbers messages and is overloading the system. What is the right change?
choices: Broadcast presence to every contact less often
Subscribe to presence only for chats on screen, debounce status changes
quiz.why: Presence is the noisiest and least important signal, so push it only to current subscribers.

quiz.q: A message to a 500-member group triggers 500 separate registry lookups and pushes. How do you make it cheaper?
choices: Look up all members in one Redis pipeline and send one frame per gateway with its local recipients
Assign one sequence number per member
quiz.why: Batching by gateway turns hundreds of pushes into a few frames.

quiz.q: The team adds end-to-end encryption. Which feature stops working server-side?
quiz.why: Routing, ordering and receipts use metadata; search and moderation need the plaintext.
